task_area: Health Maintenance, Patient Education, and Preventive Measures
front: Which older adults should be offered exercise to prevent falls?
bottom: Community-dwelling adults 65 and older who are at increased risk.

bullets.clue: A prior fall or a gait or balance problem raises risk.
bullets.treat: USPSTF 2024: recommend exercise. Multifactorial interventions are an individual decision.
bullets.trap: Do not start vitamin D solely to prevent falls in community-dwelling adults.

back: Community-dwelling adults 65 and older who are at increased risk. Key clue: A prior fall or a gait or balance problem raises risk. First-line: USPSTF 2024: recommend exercise. Multifactorial interventions are an individual decision. Exam trap: Do not start vitamin D solely to prevent falls in community-dwelling adults.

diagram.alt: Community-dwelling adults 65 and older who are at increased risk.

source.guideline: USPSTF Recommendation: Interventions to Prevent Falls in Community-Dwelling Older Adults
source.recommendation: Strongly recommended: exercise, weight loss (knee/hip, overweight), self-efficacy programs, oral NSAIDs, topical NSAIDs (knee), intra-articular glucocorticoids (knee/hip). Conditionally recommended: topical NSAIDs (hand), intra-articular steroid (hand), tramadol (when NSAIDs contraindicated or ineffective; preferred over non-tramadol opioids). Strongly against glucosamine (all sites) and chondroitin (knee/hip). Topical NSAIDs should be considered before oral NSAIDs.

front: What process damages the joint in rheumatoid arthritis, and what is first-line disease-modifying therapy?
bottom: Synovial inflammation erodes cartilage and bone.

bullets.clue: Anti-CCP antibodies are specific. Rheumatoid factor is not.
bullets.treat: ACR 2021: methotrexate is the first DMARD. Add folic acid. Screen for TB and hepatitis B before a biologic.
bullets.trap: Do not combine two biologic agents.

back: Synovial inflammation erodes cartilage and bone. Key clue: Anti-CCP antibodies are specific. Rheumatoid factor is not. First-line: ACR 2021: methotrexate is the first DMARD. Add folic acid. Screen for TB and hepatitis B before a biologic. Exam trap: Do not combine two biologic agents.

diagram.alt: Synovial inflammation erodes cartilage and bone.

source.guideline: 2021 ACR Guideline for the Treatment of Rheumatoid Arthritis
source.recommendation: DMARD-naive, moderate-to-high activity: methotrexate monotherapy strongly recommended over hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine, bDMARD or tsDMARD monotherapy, and over methotrexate plus non-TNF biologic. Short-term (<3 months) glucocorticoids only when needed at the lowest dose; against long-term (≥3 months) glucocorticoids. Treat-to-target; add bDMARD or tsDMARD when not at target on methotrexate.

task_area: History Taking and Performing Physical Examination
front: Acute monoarthritis: which exam findings make septic arthritis likely, and what must be done before antibiotics?
bottom: Warm effusion, fever, pain on passive motion: septic arthritis until proven otherwise.

bullets.treat: Arthrocentesis before antibiotics; empiric IV vancomycin ± ceftriaxone; drainage.
bullets.trap: Crystals do not exclude infection; WBC >50,000 suggests infection.

back: Warm effusion, fever, pain on passive motion: septic arthritis until proven otherwise. Key clue: S. aureus most common. First-line: Arthrocentesis before antibiotics; empiric IV vancomycin ± ceftriaxone; drainage. Exam trap: Crystals do not exclude infection; WBC >50,000 suggests infection.

diagram.alt: Septic arthritis with a knee effusion. Aspirate the joint for cell count, Gram stain, culture and crystals before IV antibiotics, then drain; crystals do not exclude infection.

source.guideline: Standard teaching; BSR/BHPR Guideline for Management of the Hot Swollen Joint in Adults; EULAR-endorsed (still current as of 2026)
source.recommendation: Hot swollen joint: aspirate before antibiotics; send synovial fluid for Gram stain, culture, cell count and crystals; blood cultures; empiric IV antibiotics guided by risk (vancomycin for MRSA risk, add a third-generation cephalosporin for gram-negative/gonococcal risk); joint drainage. Crystals do not exclude infection.

task_area: History Taking and Performing Physical Examination
front: Acute low back pain: which history and exam red flags mean emergency imaging, and when is none needed?
bottom: Saddle anesthesia, urinary retention or bilateral weakness: cauda equina, emergency MRI.

bullets.clue: Also cancer, fever, trauma, IV drug use, weight loss, progressive deficit.
bullets.treat: Stay active; heat, NSAIDs or muscle relaxants.
bullets.trap: Early imaging without red flags does not help.

back: Saddle anesthesia, urinary retention or bilateral weakness: cauda equina, emergency MRI. Key clue: Also cancer, fever, trauma, IV drug use, weight loss, progressive deficit. First-line: Stay active; heat, NSAIDs or muscle relaxants. Exam trap: Early imaging without red flags does not help.

diagram.alt: Low back pain with a disc compressing nerve roots. No imaging without red flags; heat, NSAIDs and staying active first; urgent MRI and decompression for cauda equina signs.

source.guideline: ACP Clinical Practice Guideline: Noninvasive Treatments for Acute, Subacute, and Chronic Low Back Pain (2017); ACR Appropriateness Criteria Low Back Pain (2021) (still current as of 2026)
source.recommendation: ACP 2017: acute/subacute LBP: nonpharmacologic first (superficial heat, massage, acupuncture, spinal manipulation); if drugs desired, NSAIDs or skeletal muscle relaxants. Chronic: exercise, multidisciplinary rehabilitation, CBT and others; then NSAIDs, then tramadol or duloxetine. ACR 2021 update: imaging usually not appropriate for acute LBP without red flags; MRI appropriate for suspected cauda equina, cancer, infection or immunosuppression.

task_area: Health Maintenance, Patient Education, and Preventive Measures
front: Postmenopausal woman: who gets osteoporosis screening, what T-score is diagnostic, and first-line drug?
bottom: DXA at 65, or younger with risk.

bullets.treat: Bisphosphonate (alendronate) first; calcium, vitamin D, weight-bearing exercise.
bullets.trap: Bisphosphonates need upright posture 30 minutes; check renal function.

back: DXA at 65, or younger with risk. Key clue: T-score ≤ −2.5 or a fragility fracture. First-line: Bisphosphonate (alendronate) first; calcium, vitamin D, weight-bearing exercise. Exam trap: Bisphosphonates need upright posture 30 minutes; check renal function.

diagram.alt: Osteoporosis screening with DXA in women 65 and older and younger postmenopausal women at increased risk; T-score of minus 2.5 or lower or a fragility fracture is osteoporosis, and bisphosphonates are first-line.

source.guideline: USPSTF Osteoporosis to Prevent Fractures: Screening (2025); ACP Pharmacologic Treatment of Primary Osteoporosis (2023)
source.recommendation: USPSTF Jan 2025: screen women ≥65 (B) and postmenopausal women <65 at increased risk by clinical risk assessment (B) with DXA BMD ± fracture risk assessment; men: I statement. ACP 2023: bisphosphonates first-line for primary osteoporosis; denosumab second-line; romosozumab or teriparatide, followed by a bisphosphonate, for women with very high fracture risk.

front: Older adult falls, then has a shortened, externally rotated leg: diagnosis, imaging, and timing of surgery?

bullets.clue: Shortened, externally rotated leg after a fall.
bullets.treat: X-ray (MRI if negative); surgery within 24–48 h; VTE prophylaxis.
bullets.trap: Displaced femoral neck fracture risks avascular necrosis: arthroplasty.

back: Hip fracture: surgery within 24–48 hours. Key clue: Shortened, externally rotated leg after a fall. First-line: X-ray (MRI if negative); surgery within 24–48 h; VTE prophylaxis. Exam trap: Displaced femoral neck fracture risks avascular necrosis: arthroplasty.

diagram.alt: Hip fracture through the femoral neck. X-ray, then MRI if occult; surgery within 24 to 48 hours; arthroplasty for displaced femoral neck fractures; VTE prophylaxis afterwards.

source.guideline: AAOS Clinical Practice Guideline: Management of Hip Fractures in Older Adults (2021)
source.recommendation: Surgery within 24–48 h of admission may be associated with better outcomes (moderate, upgraded). VTE prophylaxis should be used (strong). No routine preoperative traction. MRI for suspected occult fracture; arthroplasty for unstable (displaced) femoral neck fractures.

task_area: History Taking and Performing Physical Examination
front: Ankle sprain or knee injury: when is an X-ray needed, and which tests check the ACL and meniscus?
bottom: Ottawa rules decide who needs an X-ray.

bullets.clue: Bone tenderness at malleolus tip, or cannot bear weight.
bullets.treat: Ankle sprain: early functional support and exercise. ACL: Lachman; meniscus: McMurray; MRI confirms.
bullets.trap: Lachman is the most sensitive ACL test.

back: Ottawa rules decide who needs an X-ray. Key clue: Bone tenderness at malleolus tip, or cannot bear weight. First-line: Ankle sprain: early functional support and exercise. ACL: Lachman; meniscus: McMurray; MRI confirms. Exam trap: Lachman is the most sensitive ACL test.

diagram.alt: Ottawa ankle rules: X-ray for bone tenderness at the posterior malleolus, navicular or fifth metatarsal, or inability to bear weight for four steps. Lachman tests the ACL, McMurray the meniscus, and MRI confirms.

source.guideline: Ottawa Ankle Rules (Stiell, JAMA 1993); ACR Appropriateness Criteria: Acute Trauma to the Ankle and Knee (still current as of 2026)
source.recommendation: Ottawa ankle rules: ankle radiographs if malleolar-zone pain plus bone tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of either malleolus, or inability to bear weight both immediately and in the ED (4 steps); foot series for navicular or fifth metatarsal base tenderness. ACR: Ottawa/Pittsburgh rules guide radiography; MRI for suspected internal derangement.

task_area: History Taking and Performing Physical Examination
front: Shoulder pain with overhead activity and night pain: impingement or rotator cuff tear? How to tell?
bottom: Rotator cuff: weakness suggests a tear.

bullets.clue: Painful arc, positive Neer and Hawkins; drop-arm sign.
bullets.treat: Physical therapy; single steroid injection short term; MRI or ultrasound; repair if needed.
bullets.trap: Frozen shoulder loses passive motion; cuff problems keep it.

back: Rotator cuff: weakness suggests a tear. Key clue: Painful arc, positive Neer and Hawkins; drop-arm sign. First-line: Physical therapy; single steroid injection short term; MRI or ultrasound; repair if needed. Exam trap: Frozen shoulder loses passive motion; cuff problems keep it.

diagram.alt: Rotator cuff disease involving the supraspinatus tendon. Physical therapy and a single steroid injection first, MRI or ultrasound if weakness suggests a tear, and surgical repair when needed; frozen shoulder loses passive motion too.

source.guideline: AAOS Clinical Practice Guideline: Management of Rotator Cuff Injuries (2025)
source.recommendation: AAOS Aug 2025: physical therapy improves outcomes in symptomatic full-thickness tears (tear may progress over 5–10 years); combine clinical tests rather than rely on one; MRI, MRA, CT and ultrasound are useful adjuncts (strong); a single corticosteroid injection with local anesthetic may improve short-term pain and function; surgical repair yields better outcomes than nonoperative care in healed repairs; routine acromioplasty not suggested.

front: Young woman with malar rash, arthritis and a positive ANA: likely diagnosis, specific tests, and drug for everyone?

bullets.clue: Malar rash, arthritis, serositis, cytopenias, proteinuria.
bullets.treat: ANA screen; anti-dsDNA, anti-Smith specific. Hydroxychloroquine; steroids as bridge.

back: SLE: hydroxychloroquine for all. Key clue: Malar rash, arthritis, serositis, cytopenias, proteinuria. First-line: ANA screen; anti-dsDNA, anti-Smith specific. Hydroxychloroquine; steroids as bridge. Exam trap: Hydroxychloroquine needs retinal screening.

diagram.alt: Systemic lupus erythematosus: ANA is sensitive and anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith are specific. Hydroxychloroquine for all patients, steroids as a bridge kept at 5 mg or less, and steroid-sparing drugs or nephritis therapy as needed.

source.guideline: EULAR Recommendations for the Management of SLE: 2023 Update; 2019 EULAR/ACR SLE Classification Criteria
source.recommendation: HCQ for all patients unless contraindicated, target 5 mg/kg real body weight/day, individualized for flare and retinal toxicity risk. Glucocorticoids as bridging therapy, reduced to ≤5 mg/day prednisone maintenance and withdrawn when possible. Prompt immunosuppressants (methotrexate, azathioprine, mycophenolate) and/or biologics (anifrolumab, belimumab). Lupus nephritis: glucocorticoids plus mycophenolate or low-dose IV cyclophosphamide as anchor drugs. 2019 classification requires ANA ≥1:80 as entry criterion.

task_area: History Taking and Performing Physical Examination
front: Patient over 50 with shoulder and hip girdle stiffness or a new headache: which findings suggest PMR versus giant cell arteritis?
bottom: PMR: girdle stiffness, high ESR. GCA: new headache, jaw claudication, vision loss.

bullets.treat: PMR: prednisone 12.5–25 mg. GCA: high-dose steroids now.
bullets.trap: Suspected GCA: do not wait for biopsy before steroids.

back: PMR: girdle stiffness, high ESR. GCA: new headache, jaw claudication, vision loss. Key clue: Age over 50, high ESR. First-line: PMR: prednisone 12.5–25 mg. GCA: high-dose steroids now. Exam trap: Suspected GCA: do not wait for biopsy before steroids.

diagram.alt: Polymyalgia rheumatica and giant cell arteritis in adults over 50 with high ESR. PMR uses prednisone 12.5 to 25 mg; GCA needs high-dose steroids immediately, temporal artery biopsy within 2 weeks, and tocilizumab as a steroid-sparing option.

source.guideline: 2021 ACR/Vasculitis Foundation Guideline for GCA and Takayasu Arteritis; 2015 EULAR/ACR Recommendations for Polymyalgia Rheumatica
source.recommendation: GCA 2021: temporal artery biopsy within 2 weeks of starting oral glucocorticoids; unilateral, >1 cm; biopsy over ultrasound or MRI in the US; oral glucocorticoids with tocilizumab conditionally over glucocorticoids alone (methotrexate or steroids alone acceptable). PMR 2015: initial prednisone 12.5–25 mg/day, individualized taper.

front: Pediatric hip: obese teen with knee pain and limp, active boy age 4–8, or a newborn with a hip clunk?

bullets.clue: Teen obese: SCFE. Age 4–8: Perthes. Newborn: Ortolani, Barlow.
bullets.treat: SCFE: no weight bearing, surgical pinning. DDH: imaging, brace if unstable. Perthes: observe, brace.
bullets.trap: Knee pain in a child can come from the hip.

back: SCFE, Legg-Calvé-Perthes, DDH. Key clue: Teen obese: SCFE. Age 4–8: Perthes. Newborn: Ortolani, Barlow. First-line: SCFE: no weight bearing, surgical pinning. DDH: imaging, brace if unstable. Perthes: observe, brace. Exam trap: Knee pain in a child can come from the hip.

diagram.alt: Three pediatric hip disorders: slipped capital femoral epiphysis in obese teens treated with surgical pinning, Legg-Calvé-Perthes avascular necrosis at age 4 to 8, and developmental hip dysplasia in newborns found by Ortolani and Barlow and treated with a Pavlik harness.

source.guideline: AAOS Clinical Practice Guideline: Management of Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip in Infants up to Six Months (2022); standard teaching for SCFE and Perthes
source.recommendation: AAOS DDH: imaging (ultrasound) before 6 months for infants with risk factors (breech, family history) or an abnormal exam; no universal ultrasound screening; ultrasound <6 weeks may guide bracing of an unstable hip; AP pelvis X-ray instead of ultrasound from 4 months; re-examine at visits before 6 months; bracing for unstable hips (the CPG does not name Pavlik as preferred). AAP 2016 clinical report on DDH evaluation. SCFE and Perthes management is standard teaching.

task_area: History Taking and Performing Physical Examination
front: Pain out of proportion after a tibial fracture or crush injury: which exam findings confirm compartment syndrome?
bottom: Pain on passive stretch, tense compartment, pain out of proportion.

bullets.clue: Tibial fracture, crush injury or tight cast.
bullets.treat: Remove cast or dressing, limb at heart level; urgent fasciotomy.
bullets.trap: Pulses often stay present; pulselessness is late.

back: Pain on passive stretch, tense compartment, pain out of proportion. Key clue: Tibial fracture, crush injury or tight cast. First-line: Remove cast or dressing, limb at heart level; urgent fasciotomy. Exam trap: Pulses often stay present; pulselessness is late.

diagram.alt: Acute compartment syndrome with swollen lower-leg compartments after a fracture or crush injury. Split the cast, keep the limb at heart level, measure pressure if unclear, and perform emergency fasciotomy; pulses are often preserved.

source.guideline: AAOS Clinical Practice Guideline: Management of Acute Compartment Syndrome (2025 rapid update)
source.recommendation: AAOS 2025: intracompartmental pressure monitoring assists diagnosis (moderate); repeated/continuous monitoring with diastolic BP minus compartment pressure >30 mmHg helps rule out ACS (moderate); no single absolute pressure cutoff; serial clinical exam helps rule in (limited); obtunded patients: repeated or continuous pressure measurement until diagnosed or excluded (consensus).

front: Diabetic foot ulcer that probes to bone, or bone pain with fever: diagnosis, best imaging, and confirmation?

bullets.clue: Probe-to-bone positive, high ESR, ulcer over 2 cm.
bullets.treat: X-ray first, MRI if unclear; bone culture guides 6 weeks of antibiotics.
bullets.trap: Early X-ray can be normal for 2 weeks.

back: Osteomyelitis: MRI, then bone biopsy. Key clue: Probe-to-bone positive, high ESR, ulcer over 2 cm. First-line: X-ray first, MRI if unclear; bone culture guides 6 weeks of antibiotics. Exam trap: Early X-ray can be normal for 2 weeks.

diagram.alt: Osteomyelitis with a lytic bone focus. Plain X-ray first, MRI if unclear, bone biopsy and culture to guide about 6 weeks of antibiotics; early X-ray can be normal.

source.guideline: IWGDF/IDSA Guidelines on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Diabetes-related Foot Infections (2023)
source.recommendation: Suspected diabetic foot osteomyelitis: combine probe-to-bone, ESR/CRP and plain X-ray; MRI when diagnosis remains uncertain; bone culture (percutaneous or surgical) for diagnosis and to guide therapy; ~6 weeks antibiotics without resection (up to 3 weeks after minor amputation with positive bone margin).

front: Teen with night bone pain relieved by NSAIDs, vs widespread pain with fatigue and normal labs: diagnoses?

bullets.clue: Night pain relieved by NSAIDs; widespread pain with normal labs.
bullets.treat: Bone pain: X-ray; sunburst or onion-skin needs referral. Fibromyalgia: exercise, then duloxetine or pregabalin.
bullets.trap: Fibromyalgia has normal ESR, CRP and exam strength.

back: Osteoid osteoma vs fibromyalgia. Key clue: Night pain relieved by NSAIDs; widespread pain with normal labs. First-line: Bone pain: X-ray; sunburst or onion-skin needs referral. Fibromyalgia: exercise, then duloxetine or pregabalin. Exam trap: Fibromyalgia has normal ESR, CRP and exam strength.

diagram.alt: Bone tumors versus fibromyalgia: osteosarcoma has a sunburst pattern, Ewing sarcoma onion skinning, and osteoid osteoma a nidus with night pain relieved by NSAIDs; fibromyalgia has widespread pain with normal labs and is treated with exercise first.

source.guideline: 2016 ACR Fibromyalgia Diagnostic Criteria (Wolfe et al.); EULAR Revised Recommendations for Fibromyalgia Management (2017); standard teaching for bone tumors (still current as of 2026)
source.recommendation: EULAR 2017: exercise is the only strong recommendation; then psychological therapies; drugs (low-dose amitriptyline, duloxetine or milnacipran, pregabalin, tramadol) for severe pain or sleep disturbance; against NSAIDs (as monotherapy), strong opioids and corticosteroids. ACR 2016: widespread pain index and symptom severity, symptoms ≥3 months. Bone tumor imaging patterns are standard teaching.
